subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. They do not paint with a brush — instead they give a device a careful set of instructions, and the device draws a shape or walks a path shaped like a letter. When the instructions are right, a picture appears. That is the art. The first big idea is the algorithm — a set of instructions in the right order. To make a drawing, the device needs simple commands: marker down (start drawing), move forward (go straight), turn left or turn right (make a corner), and stop. If you draw the little foot of a letter L before the tall line, you get the wrong shape. The second big idea is programming a device. Some devices can move. We write instructions and the device follows them — a little robot on the floor, or a character on a screen. The clever part, and the reason this is an art unit, is that the path the device travels can make a picture or a letter. Programming a robot to walk in the shape of a C or an L is drawing with movement.

outcomes: Write and follow an algorithm — a set of drawing instructions in the correct order.
Use the drawing commands: Marker down, Marker up, Move forward, Turn left, Turn right and Stop program.
Explain, in their own words, why the order of the steps matters.
Program a device — a floor robot on a grid, or a ScratchJr character — to follow a path.
See and say that a path can make a picture or a letter (that is the art).
Use Repeat to make an algorithm shorter when a step happens again and again, and know the result is the same.
Run or act out a program, check whether it did what they wanted, and fix a command that is wrong.

concepts.title: Be the marker: an algorithm that draws (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: An algorithm is a set of instructions in the right order. To draw, a device follows commands. The most important one today is marker down — it means “put the pen on the paper and start drawing”. Then Move forward makes a line. I am going to be a drawing robot. But I only do what you tell me, one command at a time. draw a line. How far? Which way?
concepts.example: And my marker is still up, so nothing happens! Now you can give you clean commands and follow them exactly
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that Marker down must come before drawing, and that Move forward needs a direction and a number? Do you follow the commands in order?

concepts.title: Turns make corners: drawing a letter (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: A turn makes a corner. Turn left and Turn right each turn a quarter — like turning to face the side of the room. A turn happens on the spot; it does not move you forward. By joining Move forward and turns, we can draw a whole letter. Stand everyone up. Face the front together. “Turn right!” — everyone makes a quarter turn. “Turn right again!” — now facing the back.
concepts.example: Feel how a turn changes the way we face but does not move us anywhere. Start with the marker at the top, facing down.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know a turn does not move the marker forward? Can you order the steps so the letter comes out right? Can you pick the correct turn to make the corner go the right way?

concepts.title: Program a robot on the floor grid (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: Some devices can move. We can program them — write instructions and you can follow. And here is the art: the path can be the shape of a letter. Make a big grid on the floor with masking tape, about four squares by four squares. Then, together, program the robot to walk a path shaped like an L. Choose one child (or a soft toy) to be the robot, standing on a square and facing one way.
concepts.example: Explain the three robot commands: Move forward 1 (step into the next square), Turn left, Turn right. Start the robot at the top, facing down the grid.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a turn changes the facing but is not a step forward? Can you predict, or recognise, the letter the path makes? Can you give clear, single commands in order?

concepts.title: Repeat: a shorter way (floor grid, then ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
When we do the same step again and again, we can use Repeat. It makes our algorithm shorter, and the result is exactly the same. Fewer steps, same path.

Go back to the floor grid. To walk four squares straight, we wrote Move forward 1 four times.
concepts.example: That is a lot of writing. Watch — we can say it in a shorter way.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that Repeat gives the same result as writing the step many times? Can you build a Repeat block in ScratchJr and run it? Can you spot a step that is repeated?

concepts.title: Be an artist: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
They plan an algorithm for a letter, make it (as the marker, on the floor grid, or in ScratchJr), use Repeat to shorten a straight part, then check and fix it. This session and the Mini-Project go hand in hand.

Now you are the artist. You will make a letter with code for our Ehel Academy display.
concepts.example: First plan your steps, then make it, then check it works — and if a command is wrong, find it and fix it. Keep letters simple — L, C, T or I are perfect.
concepts.checkYourself: Does your letter come out roughly right? Did you use a Repeat? Did you find and fix the wrong command? Do you plan before making?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

selfAssessment: I can write and follow an algorithm — a set of drawing instructions in the correct order.
I can use the drawing commands: Marker down, Marker up, Move forward, Turn left, Turn right and Stop program.
I can explain, in their own words, why the order of the steps matters.
I can program a device — a floor robot on a grid, or a ScratchJr character — to follow a path.
I can see and say that a path can make a picture or a letter (that is the art).
I can use Repeat to make an algorithm shorter when a step happens again and again, and know the result is the same.
I can run or act out a program, check whether it did what they wanted, and fix a command that is wrong.
